body.translated_text: Homage to <s>Mañjuśrī</s>, the eternally youthful one!

children.translated_text: The imagined (<s>parikalpita</s>), the dependent (<s>paratantra</s>), and the perfected (<s>pariniṣpanna</s>) —
these three natures (<s>svabhāva</s>) are held to be the profound object of knowledge for the wise. // 1 //

children.text: yat khyāti paratantro 'sau yathā khyāti sa kalpitaḥ /
children.translated_text: That which appears is the dependent; the manner in which it appears is the imagined —
because of its having a mode of existence dependent on conditions, and because of being a mere product of imagination. // 2 //
The perpetual non-existence of the manner in which that [dependent] appears —
that should be known as the perfected nature, because of its being otherwise invariable. // 3 //

children.text: tatra kiṃ khyātyasatkalpaḥ kathaṃ khyāti dvayātmanā /
children.translated_text: Therein, what appears? An unreal imagination. How does it appear? In the form of duality.

children.text: tasya kā nāstitā tena yā tatrādvayadharmatā // Tsn_4 //
children.translated_text: What is its non-existence? That which is the nature of non-duality therein. // 4 //
Here, 'unreal imagination' is a certain [thing]; it is by that indeed that [duality] is imagined.

children.text: yathā ca kalpayatyartha tathātyantaṃ na vidyate // Tsn_5 //
children.translated_text: And the way in which it imagines the object — in that manner it absolutely does not exist. // 5 //
In its cause-and-effect aspect, mind (<s>citta</s>) is held to be twofold:

children.text: yadālayākhyaṃ vijñānaṃ pravṛttyākhyaṃ ca saptadhā // Tsn_6 //
children.translated_text: that which is called <s>ālaya-vijñāna</s> (storehouse consciousness), and that called <s>pravṛtti</s> (active), which is sevenfold. // 6 //
Because it is variegated (<s>citra</s>) with the seeds of the impressions of defilement, it is called <s>citta</s> (mind).
The first [is called citta] from that; the second, from its activity in variegated forms. // 7 //
In brief, this unreal imagination is held to be threefold:
that which is maturational (<s>vaipākika</s>), that which is occasioned (<s>naimittika</s>), and the other, that which is phenomenal (<s>prātibhāsika</s>). // 8 //
The first is the root consciousness (<s>mūlavijñāna</s>), since it is of the nature of maturation.
The other is the active consciousness (<s>pravṛttivijñāna</s>), operating as seen, seer, and cognition. // 9 //
By being existent and non-existent, by duality and unity, in defilement and purification,
and by non-difference of characteristics — the profundity of the [three] natures is taught. // 10 //
Since it is grasped as existent, yet is absolutely non-existent,
the imagined nature is therefore held to have the character of being both existent and non-existent. // 11 //
It exists in the mode of delusion, yet as it appears it does not exist —
therefore the dependent is held to have the character of being both existent and non-existent. // 12 //
That which exists as non-duality, and which is the very absence of duality —
that perfected nature is therefore held to have the character of being both existent and non-existent. // 13 //
Because of the twofold nature of the imagined object and because of its non-existence as one [thing],
the imagined nature is held by the childish to have the character of duality and unity. // 14 //
Because of appearing as duality and because of being one as mere delusion,
the dependent nature is held to have the character of duality and unity. // 15 //
Because of being of the nature of the absence of duality, and because of being of one nature as non-dual,
the perfected nature is held to have the character of duality and unity. // 16 //
The imagined and the dependent should be known as the characteristic of defilement (<s>saṃkleśa</s>);
but the perfected is held to be the characteristic of purification (<s>vyavadāna</s>). // 17 //
Because of being of the nature of an unreal duality, and because of being of the nature of its absence,
the perfected should be known as of undifferentiated character from the imagined nature. // 18 //
Because of being of the nature of non-duality, and because of being of the nature of the absence of duality,
the imagined too should be understood as of undifferentiated character from the perfected. // 19 //
Because of the non-existence of the mode of appearance, and because of being of the nature of that non-existence,
the perfected is of undifferentiated character from the dependent nature. // 20 //
Because of being of the nature of an unreal duality, and because of being not of the nature of the mode of appearance,
the dependent too should be understood as of undifferentiated character from the perfected. // 21 //
The sequential distinction of the natures, from the standpoint of conventional practice,
and from the standpoint of entry into them, is established for the purpose of understanding. // 22 //
The imagined is of the nature of convention; the other is of the nature of the one who conventionally practices;
and the third is held to be of the nature of the cessation of convention. // 23 //
First, the dependent, which is of the nature of the absence of duality, is entered;
then, therein, the imagined — a mere imagination, an unreal duality — is entered. // 24 //
Then, the existence of the absence of duality, the perfected, is entered here;

children.text: tathā hyasāveva tadā astināstīti cocyate // Tsn_25 //
children.translated_text: for thus indeed, at that time, that very [thing] is said to both exist and not exist. // 25 //
All three of these natures indeed have the characteristic of being based on non-duality —
because of non-existence, because of not being so, and because of being of the nature of their absence. // 26 //
Just as a magical creation (<s>māyā</s>), produced by a spell, appears in the form of an elephant —

children.text: ākāramātraṃ tatrāsti hastī nāsti tu sarvathā // Tsn_27 //
children.translated_text: there is only a mere form there; the elephant does not exist at all. // 27 //
The imagined nature is the elephant; the dependent is its form;
that which is the absence of the elephant therein — that is held to be the perfected. // 28 //
The unreal conceptualization (<s>asatkalpa</s>) thus appears from the root-consciousness (<s>mūlacitta</s>) in the form of duality;
the duality absolutely does not exist there — there exists only a mere form [of appearance]. (29)
The root-consciousness (<s>mūlavijñāna</s>) is to be understood as like a <s>mantra</s> [in a magic show]; suchness (<s>tathatā</s>) is considered like the [piece of] wood;
conceptualization (<s>vikalpa</s>) is to be regarded as like the elephant-form; duality is like the [real] elephant. (30)
In the penetration of the reality of the object, the three characteristics [are understood] simultaneously:

children.text: parijñā ca prahāṇaṃ ca prāptiśceṣṭā yathākramam // Tsn_31 //
children.translated_text: full understanding (<s>parijñā</s>), abandonment (<s>prahāṇa</s>), and attainment (<s>prāpti</s>) — these are desired in that order. (31)
Full understanding is the non-apprehension (<s>anupalambha</s>) here; abandonment is considered to be non-appearance (<s>akhyāna</s>);

children.text: upalambhanimittā tu prāptiḥ sākṣātkriyāpi sā // Tsn_32 //
children.translated_text: attainment, however, [arises] from the cause of apprehension — that too is direct realization (<s>sākṣātkṛti</s>). (32)
Through the non-apprehension of duality, the aspect of duality disappears;
through its disappearance, the perfected [nature] (<s>niṣpanna</s>) — the absence of duality — is realized. (33)
The non-apprehension of the elephant, the disappearance of its form,

children.text: upalambhaśca kāṣṭhasya māyāyāṃ yugapad yathā // Tsn_34 //
children.translated_text: and the apprehension of the [piece of] wood — in the magical illusion (<s>māyā</s>), [these occur] simultaneously, just so. (34)
Because of blocking contradictory cognitions, because of seeing the futility [of duality] through wisdom,
and because of the continuity of the three knowledges — the attainment of liberation is effortless. (35)
Through the apprehension of mind-only (<s>cittamātra</s>), [there arises] the non-apprehension of the object of knowledge;
through the non-apprehension of the object of knowledge, there would be the non-apprehension of [even] mind. (36)
Through the non-apprehension of both, there arises the apprehension of the <s>dharmadhātu</s> (realm of reality);
through the apprehension of the <s>dharmadhātu</s>, there would be the apprehension of sovereign power (<s>vibhutva</s>). (37)
And one who has apprehended sovereign power, through the accomplishment of the aims of self and others,
the wise one attains the unsurpassed <s>bodhi</s> (enlightenment), whose essence is the three bodies (<s>trikāya</s>). (38)

body.translated_text: Thus the <s>Trisvabhāvanirdeśa</s> (Treatise on the Three Natures) is completed.
